claim: Dante said this Pisan count ate his children. Seven centuries later, his ribs testified.

knots.passage: This bell is older than the bell-chamber itself, and comes from the tower Vergata in Palazzo Pretorio in Pisa, where it was called La Giustizia (The Justice). The bell was tolled to announce executions of criminals and traitors, including Count Ugolino in 1289.
knots.hatnote: One of the tower's seven bells had a darker first job.

knots.passage: The archbishop, accusing Ugolino of treachery, aroused the citizens. When the town hall was set on fire, Ugolino surrendered. While his illegitimate son was killed, Ugolino himself – together with his sons Gaddo and Uguccione and his grandsons Nino (surnamed "the Brigand") and Anselmuccio – were detained in the Muda, a tower belonging to the Gualandi family. In March 1289, on orders of the archbishop, who had proclaimed himself podestà, the keys were thrown into the Arno river and the prisoners left to starve.
knots.hatnote: Pisa's ruler fell in 1288, and his punishment was another tower.

knots.passage: According to Dante, the prisoners were slowly starved to death and before dying Ugolino's children begged him to eat their bodies.
knots.hatnote: Dante, a contemporary, put the story into the Inferno.

knots.passage: Ugolino's statement that hunger proved stronger than grief has been interpreted in two ways, either that Ugolino devoured his offspring's corpses after being driven mad with hunger, or that starvation killed him after he had failed to die of grief. The first and more ghastly of these interpretations has proved the more popular and resonant.
knots.hatnote: One ambiguous line made him the 'Cannibal Count' for centuries.

knots.passage: In 2002, paleoanthropologist Francesco Mallegni conducted DNA testing on the recently excavated bodies of Ugolino and his children. His analysis agrees with the remains being a father, his sons and his grandsons. Additional comparison to DNA from modern-day members of the Gherardesca family leave Mallegni about 98 percent sure that he has identified the remains correctly. However, the forensic analysis discredits the allegation of cannibalism. Analysis of the rib bones of the Ugolino skeleton reveals traces of magnesium, but no zinc, implying he had consumed no meat in the months before his death.
knots.hatnote: Then, in 2002, the bones themselves were questioned.

knots.passage: In 2007, Mallegni gave Dante's image a new 3D look. The new face shows softer traits: large eyes, a rounded jaw and a gentler expression, although the nose remains crooked.
knots.hatnote: The scientist had one more medieval face to rebuild.

payoff: The scientist whose chemistry cleared Ugolino of cannibalism went on to rebuild the face of Dante, the poet who accused him.
caveats: In 2008 Tuscany's archival superintendent disputed Mallegni's findings, claiming the burial documents were Fascist-era forgeries (noted on Ugolino's page).
Ugolino's page notes the cannibalism reading comes from interpreting one of Dante's lines; Dante never states it outright.
